extracted.intended_audience: early-modern natural philosophers and experimental chemists (readers of Boyle's Sceptical Chymist)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating chemical analyses and elemental claims
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for judging whether substances obtained by analysis (especially by fire) are genuine elementary principles, and for designing and interpreting experiments of chemical analysis. Focus is on the limits of fire, alternative methods, reproducibility, and careful attribution of products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of fire as an analyzer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fire is not an universal, adæquate, and sufficient instrument to analyze mixt bodies into their hypostatical principles; it commonly only disposes parts into new textures rather than analyzes into true elementary principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that products obtained by exposing a compound to fire are its true elements. Examples: many metals and minerals resist true separation by fire; fire may only pulverize or change texture. Use caution before generalizing from fiery analyses to claims about elemental composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products obtained by analysis may be produced de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not so sure that every seemingly similar or distinct substance separated from a body by the help of the Fire was pre-existent in it as a principle; some substances obtainable by fire may be 'produced de novo' by the operation of the fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone claims an analysis reveals pre-existing ingredients, require evidence that the separated substances existed in the same form prior to heating. Prefer additional arguments beyond the mere fact of separation by fire to establish elementarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative separation methods and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Other agents and methods (gentle heat, solar distillation, dunghills, menstruums such as the Alkahest) can separate substances from concretes and may yield different substances than common fire does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test multiple methods (e.g., gentle bath, solar or biological decomposition, specialized solvents) because different instruments can yield distinct products; a method that yields new or different substances weakens the claim that fire-given products are the definitive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the role of additaments and menstruums
rubrics_metrics.description: When any menstruum or additament is employed together with fire to obtain a sulphur or salt, one must examine whether the menstruum merely assists in collecting a particle already extricated by the fire, or whether a coalition occurs between parts of the body and parts of the menstruum so that the product results from their union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design controls to determine whether the solvent/additament is inert (only assembling what fire separated) or chemically participates. If the product may be the result of union with the menstruum, it should not be accepted uncritically as a native element of the original body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volatility/fixity separations do not imply elementarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fire often separates parts by differences of volatility or fixity rather than by revealing pure elementary substances; the order and coexistence of distillates reflect volatility, texture, and relative gravity, not necessarily distinct elementary natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret distillation fractions cautiously: similar volatility can cause components to ascend together and later separate by settling, not because they are distinct elements. Use additional analytical evidence to claim a fraction is an elementary principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire can unite as well as separate
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes fire, instead of separating, combines disparate ingredients into new, more stubbornly united bodies (e.g., vitrification, formation of glass) that resist further separation by fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether heat causes irreversible unions; do not presume that heating always reveals constituent parts. Examples: production of glass from sand and alkali; formation of solid fused masses where components become inseparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold and other non-ignitive processes can separate components but are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Extream cold can sometimes separate aqueous and spirituous parts (Congregare Homogenea & Segregare Heterogenea by cold), as in some frozen beers or in certain decoctions, but this is not universally reliable and depends on circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tests using cold (freezing) as an alternative separation technique, but verify repeatability and scope: some liquors resist the separation, and success may be rare or conditional (examples: Dutch Nova Zembla beer account; Paracelsian freezing of wine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer eyewitness, reproducible experiments over appeals to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony and authority are insufficient: 'He that hath seen it hath more reason to beleeve it, than He that hath not'; rely on credible eye‑witnesses and reproducible trials rather than untested reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand reproducible demonstrations; treat singular or improbable reports (even by famous authors like Helmont or Paracelsus) with skepticism until experiment corroborates them. Where possible, perform or obtain independent repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graded degrees of heat as an analytical tool with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Different degrees of heat carry over different volatile principles in order; graded heat can separate additional components (e.g., spirit, oil, salts) but this separation reflects gradations of volatility not necessarily true elementary distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ incremental heating to fractionate mixtures and observe order of escapement, but avoid concluding elemental identity from such sequences alone. Document which fractions co-distil and how they rearrange on condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful experimental procedure, measurement, and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments must be carefully controlled and measured (e.g., drying and weighing soil before and after cultivating plants) to draw valid conclusions about material change and consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for moisture, repeat drying/heating cycles, weigh accurately, and record procedures and timings. The pumpkin/earth experiment demonstrates the need to control for drying and to re-weigh to confirm mass loss is genuine rather than residual moisture.
